title: Constructors and properties
summary: Make sure every object starts out valid, and control how its data is read and changed.

steps.title: Constructors: born ready
body: With plain fields, a new object starts empty and you hope someone fills it in. Forget one line and you have a customer with no name.
A **constructor** closes that gap. It is a special method that runs during `new`, and it can demand the data the object needs.
```csharp
Customer c = new Customer("Maya");
Console.WriteLine(c.Name);   // Maya
class Customer
public string Name;
public Customer(string name)
Name = name;
- A constructor has the **same name as the class** and **no return type**.
- Once you write one that takes parameters, `new Customer()` with no arguments stops compiling. That is the point: a customer without a name can no longer exist.
> **Tip:** This is also why the last lesson needed `= ""` on string fields. The compiler warns when a `string` could be left empty. A constructor that always sets it removes the warning properly.

steps.prompt: What happens on the first line?
options: It does not compile: the only constructor needs a `sku` and a `quantity`
It creates a line with `Sku` empty and `Quantity` 0
It compiles, then crashes when the program runs
It creates a line and asks the user for the values
steps.explain: A class only gets a free no-argument constructor when you write none yourself. Here the compiler forces every caller to supply both values.

steps.title: Properties
body: Public fields let anyone change anything at any time. C# code almost always uses **properties** instead. A property looks like a field from outside, but you decide who may read it and who may write it.
```csharp
class OrderLine
public string Sku { get; }             // read-only after construction
public int Quantity { get; set; }      // read and write
public decimal UnitPrice { get; }
public decimal Total => UnitPrice * Quantity;   // computed on every read
public OrderLine(string sku, decimal unitPrice, int quantity)
Sku = sku;
UnitPrice = unitPrice;
Quantity = quantity;
- `{ get; set; }` is an **auto-property**: C# stores the value for you.
- `{ get; }` has no setter. Only the constructor can assign it.
- `=> expression` stores nothing. `Total` is worked out fresh each time, so it can never be out of date.
You use them exactly like fields: `line.Quantity = 3;` and `line.Total`.

steps.prompt: A customer's name is fixed at creation. Their email can be changed later.
steps.explain: `{ get; }` can only be assigned in the constructor. `{ get; set; }` can be assigned by anyone, any time.

steps.prompt: `Total` is a computed property. What does this print?
code: public OrderLine(string sku, decimal unitPrice, int quantity)
steps.explain: `Total` is recalculated on every read, so it follows `Quantity` automatically. Nobody has to remember to update it.

steps.title: A cart item
prompt: - `Quantity` (`int`): `get` and `set`. A new item starts with quantity **1**.
starter: // store the values; Quantity starts at 1
template: var dojoItem = new CartItem("Mug", 8m);
Dojo.Eq("Name comes from the constructor", "Mug", dojoItem.Name);
Dojo.Eq("Price comes from the constructor", 8m, dojoItem.Price);
Dojo.Eq("Quantity starts at 1", 1, dojoItem.Quantity);
Dojo.Eq("Subtotal is 8 for one mug", 8m, dojoItem.Subtotal);
dojoItem.Quantity = 3;
Dojo.Eq("Subtotal follows Quantity (3 mugs = 24)", 24m, dojoItem.Subtotal);
Dojo.Check("Name has no setter", typeof(CartItem).GetProperty("Name")?.CanWrite == false, "Name should be a property declared as { get; }");
Dojo.Check("Price has no setter", typeof(CartItem).GetProperty("Price")?.CanWrite == false, "Price should be a property declared as { get; }");
Dojo.Check("Subtotal has no setter", typeof(CartItem).GetProperty("Subtotal")?.CanWrite == false, "Subtotal should be computed with =>");
{{CODE}}
hints: A read-only auto-property: `public string Name { get; }`. Assign it inside the constructor.
Set `Quantity = 1;` in the constructor, or write `public int Quantity { get; set; } = 1;`.
The computed one is a single line: `public decimal Subtotal => Price * Quantity;`

steps.title: Object initialisers, init and required
body: Constructors with six parameters are hard to read: which `""` was the postcode? An **object initialiser** names each value instead.
```csharp
var label = new ShippingLabel
Recipient = "Maya Okafor",
City = "Leeds"
class ShippingLabel
public required string Recipient { get; init; }
public required string City { get; init; }
public string Country { get; init; } = "UK";
- `init` is a setter that only works **while the object is being created**. Afterwards the property is read-only.
- `required` makes the compiler reject any `new ShippingLabel { ... }` that leaves the property out.
- `= "UK"` is a default. Callers may override it or skip it.
Together they give you the safety of a constructor with the readability of names.

steps.prompt: Using the `ShippingLabel` class from the card, what happens here?
code: var label = new ShippingLabel { Recipient = "Maya", City = "Leeds" };
options: Line 2 does not compile: an `init` property can only be set during creation
Line 1 does not compile: `Country` was not set
It runs and the city becomes York
It compiles, then throws an exception on line 2
steps.explain: `Country` has a default, so leaving it out is fine. `City` is `init`-only, and the compiler enforces that. No running program can ever change it.

steps.title: Validate in the constructor
body: A constructor can do more than copy values. It can **refuse** bad ones.
```csharp
public OrderLine(string sku, int quantity)
if (quantity <= 0)
throw new ArgumentException("Quantity must be positive");
Sku = sku;
Quantity = quantity;

`throw` stops the constructor on the spot. No object is created, and the caller gets an error instead of a broken order line. (Exceptions get a full lesson in the next module. For now: `throw new ArgumentException("message")` means *you gave me a bad argument*.)
This is the real payoff. If the only way to make an `OrderLine` is through a constructor that checks, then **every `OrderLine` in your program is valid**. No other code has to check again.

steps.prompt: Build the constructor: check the quantity first, then store `Sku`, then `Quantity`.
lines: throw new ArgumentException("Quantity must be positive");
steps.explain: Checks go first, so a bad value is rejected before anything is stored.

steps.title: Valid from the start
prompt: - it throws `ArgumentException` when `name` is empty or only spaces, or when `price` is negative (0 is allowed)
**`ShippingLabel`** (no constructor, used with an object initialiser)
starter: // Name, Price: get only. Stock: get and set. InStock: computed.
// refuse bad values, then store the good ones
solution: throw new ArgumentException("Price cannot be negative");
public required string Recipient { get; init; }
template: var dojoP = new Product("Tea", 2.50m);
Dojo.Eq("Name comes from the constructor", "Tea", dojoP.Name);
Dojo.Eq("Price comes from the constructor", 2.50m, dojoP.Price);
Dojo.Eq("Stock starts at 0", 0, dojoP.Stock);
Dojo.Eq("InStock is false with no stock", false, dojoP.InStock);
dojoP.Stock = 3;
Dojo.Eq("InStock is true once Stock is 3", true, dojoP.InStock);
Dojo.Check("Name has no setter", typeof(Product).GetProperty("Name")?.CanWrite == false, "Name should be declared as { get; }");
Dojo.Check("Price has no setter", typeof(Product).GetProperty("Price")?.CanWrite == false, "Price should be declared as { get; }");
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentException>("new Product(\"\", 1) throws ArgumentException", () => new Product("", 1m));
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentException>("a name of only spaces throws ArgumentException", () => new Product("   ", 1m));
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentException>("a negative price throws ArgumentException", () => new Product("Tea", -1m));
Dojo.Try("a price of 0 is allowed", () => { var free = new Product("Sample", 0m); Dojo.Eq("a price of 0 is allowed", 0m, free.Price); });
var dojoL = new ShippingLabel { Recipient = "Maya" };
Dojo.Eq("Recipient is set by the initialiser", "Maya", dojoL.Recipient);
Dojo.Eq("Country defaults to UK", "UK", dojoL.Country);
var dojoL2 = new ShippingLabel { Recipient = "Ben", Country = "FR" };
Dojo.Eq("Country can be overridden at creation", "FR", dojoL2.Country);
{{CODE}}
hints: Put the two `if (...) throw new ArgumentException("...");` checks at the top of the constructor, before any assignment.
`InStock` is a computed property: `public bool InStock => Stock > 0;`
The label properties look like `public required string Recipient { get; init; }` and `public string Country { get; init; } = "UK";`
